Pursue Idea B, the municipal water utility software. With 14 months of personal savings and a technical cofounder, you need a defensible wedge where domain expertise lowers failure risk. Idea A faces brutal competition and low moats; your letters of intent are from friends, not market validation, and seed investor interest is cheap. Conversely, your four years as a civil engineer gives you an unfair advantage in understanding messy utility data and regulatory constraints. While utilities have notoriously long sales cycles, domain authenticity allows you to bypass generic pitches and build exactly what operators will pay for.

To reduce risk in the first six months, execute a strict 90-day validation sprint before writing code. Contact five former colleagues or municipal connections outside your immediate network to map their procurement workflows and decision makers. Offer a paid pilot for a narrow scope, such as predicting failures for a single pressure zone, to test willingness to pay despite council delays. 

Material assumptions: your savings cover bare living costs for 14 months, your technical cofounder can build an MVP independently, and small utilities possess digitized asset records. 

Decision criteria to pivot: If you cannot secure at least one paid letter of intent or binding pilot agreement with a non-friend municipality by month four, or if sales cycles consistently exceed nine months without early cash flow, immediately halt development and reassess. Otherwise, leverage your deep operational insights to build a sticky, high-retention business in an underserved, recession-resistant market.
